War in Heaven
WAWR in HEV-un
n. phr. (the conflict of Michael and his angels with the dragon, and the dragon's casting out)
Greek polemos en tōiouranōi — polemos, war or battle, not a skirmish; ouranos, heaven; the outcome is given by eblthē, he was cast out, a passive naming God as the one who casts.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

“And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon; and the dragon fought and his angels, And prevailed not; neither was their place found any more in heaven.” The chapter then names the loser plainly — that great dragon, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world — and the heaven rejoices with a loud voice that the accuser of the brethren is cast down, overcome by the blood of the Lamb and the word of the saints' testimony. Three points govern the doctrine. First, the war is real but it is not even: the dragon fights and prevailed not, and the verb of his casting out is passive, which is to say God did the casting. Second, the ground of the victory named in the eleventh verse is not angelic strength but the blood of the Lamb, so the decisive event is Calvary. Third, the dragon's response is war on earth against the woman's seed, with great wrath because he knoweth that he hath but a short time — the persecution of the church is thus the rage of a defeated enemy, not the advance of a winning one. Reformed expositors have connected this casting out with Christ's own words that He beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven and that now is the prince of this world judged.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): War, a contest between nations or states carried on by force. Heaven, the region above; the dwelling of God and His holy angels. War in heaven, Revelation 12:7, the casting out of the dragon by Michael and his angels.

expand to see more

War, a contest or conflict carried on by force between opposing parties.

Heaven, the region above the earth; the dwelling place of God and His angels.

Greek polemos, a war or battle, a sustained conflict rather than a skirmish.

Greek ischyō ouk, prevailed not — of the dragon and his angels.

Overcome by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, Revelation 12:11.

Key Scripture

Rev 12:7 — "And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon; and the dragon fought and his angels,"

Rev 12:8 — "And prevailed not; neither was their place found any more in heaven."

Rev 12:9 — "And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him."

Rev 12:11 — "And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death."

Modern Corruption

The passage is turned into a cosmic dualism of two comparable powers, or else mined for a technique of spiritual combat that displaces the blood of the Lamb named as the ground of victory.

expand to see more

Popular treatments make this a battle between near-equals whose outcome hung in doubt, which is dualism and not Christianity. Scripture's dragon is a creature; he fights and prevails not; the verb of his expulsion is passive, which means God cast him out; and he operates throughout the book within limits set for him, down to the short time he is allowed. The Reformed doctrine of providence holds here as everywhere: Satan is real, powerful, and wholly under God's government, so that even his rage serves the purposes of the One who permits it.

The second error belongs to the spiritual-warfare industry, which reads the chapter as a manual — territorial spirits to be bound, strongholds to be named, formulas to be pronounced — and leaves out the eleventh verse, where the saints overcome by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony and by not loving their lives unto the death. Those are the given weapons: the atonement, confession of the truth, and willingness to die. The principle to recover is that the Christian's part in this war is faith, witness and endurance, armed with the whole armour of God which is doctrine and prayer, and that the decisive battle was fought at the cross and is not being refought now.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek polemos, war; ischyō ouk, prevailed not; the passive ‘was cast out’ names God as the agent — and Revelation 12:11 names the blood of the Lamb as the victory.

expand to see more

Greek polemos, war or battle; a sustained conflict, not a skirmish.

Greek drakōn, the dragon, named as the Devil and Satan in Revelation 12:9.

Greek ischyō, to prevail or be strong — here denied to the dragon.

Greek ekballō in the passive, was cast out; God is the unnamed agent.

Compare Satan falling as lightning from heaven, Luke 10:18.

Usage

"And there was war in heaven"

"Michael and his angels fought against the dragon"

"they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb"
